hints: Focus on what the silver nitrate test is really telling you, the colour of the precipitate and what happens in ammonia identifies the halide.
A white precipitate that dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia is the classic result for chloride, $\text{Cl}^-$, as $\text{AgCl}$.
Combine that anion with $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ to work out the correct formula of the calcium salt, then add up the atomic masses to find $M_r$.
walkthrough:
**Identify the anion from the test**

This is the test for halides. Silver ions give different silver halides with different solubilities in ammonia.

$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{X}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgX}(s)$$

**Match the observation to chloride**

White precipitate means $\text{AgCl}$ or possibly $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$, but nitric acid is added to remove carbonate. Soluble in dilute $\text{NH}_3$ confirms $\text{AgCl}$.

Cream soluble only in concentrated $\text{NH}_3$ would be bromide, yellow insoluble would be iodide. So the anion is $\text{Cl}^-$.

**Work out the calcium compound and its Mr**

Calcium is Group 2, so it forms $\text{Ca}^{2+}$. With $\text{Cl}^-$ it must be $\text{CaCl}_2$ to balance charges.

$$M_r = A_r(\text{Ca}) + 2 \times A_r(\text{Cl}) = 40.1 + 2(35.5) = 111.1$$

options.A: Too low to be any calcium chloride. This comes from a serious formula or arithmetic error, such as roughly halving the true $M_r$ of $\text{CaCl}_2$. $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ needs two $\text{Cl}^-$ ions.
options.B: 75.6 is $40.1 + 35.5$, the $M_r$ of $\text{CaCl}$. This is the common valency trap of forgetting calcium is 2+ and chloride is 1-, so two chlorides are needed, not one.
options.C: Correct. White $\text{AgCl}$ soluble in dilute ammonia proves chloride. The calcium salt is therefore $\text{CaCl}_2$, giving $M_r = 40.1 + 71.0 = 111.1$.
options.D: 199.9 is $40.1 + 2(79.9)$, the $M_r$ of $\text{CaBr}_2$. This is the trap of confusing bromide with chloride. Bromide gives a cream precipitate soluble only in concentrated ammonia, not white soluble in dilute ammonia.
